title: UNIT 2: MICROORGANISMS
notes:
✓ Microorganisms → organisms or biological agents too small to be seen clearly with the naked eye.

✓ Major groups studied in microbiology → Bacteria, Archaea, Fungi, Protozoa, Algae, Viruses and microscopic stages of Helminths.

✓ Microbiology → study of microorganisms.

✓ Microorganisms occur in almost every environment and have important roles in health, agriculture, industry and ecosystems.

title: 2.1 CLASSIFICATION OF MICROORGANISMS
notes:
✓ Based on evolutionary relationships, organisms are grouped into three domains:

1 Bacteria → prokaryotic organisms.

2 Archaea → prokaryotic organisms distinct from bacteria.

3 Eukarya → organisms with eukaryotic cells.

✓ Microbiology mainly studies microorganisms from all three domains.

title: 2.1.1 BACTERIA — GENERAL CHARACTERISTICS
notes:
✓ Bacteria → unicellular prokaryotic organisms.

◆ No membrane-bound nucleus.
◆ DNA is located in the nucleoid region.
◆ Usually reproduce asexually by cell division.
◆ Very diverse in shape, nutrition and metabolism.
◆ Some are beneficial while others cause disease.
◆ Some bacteria can form endospores for survival under unfavorable conditions.

title: 2.1.2 STRUCTURE OF A BACTERIAL CELL
notes:
✓ Important bacterial structures:

◆ Capsule/slime layer → protection and attachment.

◆ Cell wall → maintains shape and protects the cell.

◆ Cell membrane → controls movement of substances.

◆ Cytoplasm → site of many metabolic reactions.

◆ Nucleoid → contains main bacterial DNA.

◆ Plasmid → small circular DNA carrying additional genes.

◆ Ribosomes → protein synthesis.

◆ Fimbriae → attachment to surfaces.

◆ Flagella → movement.

◆ Endospore → resistant survival structure in some bacteria.

title: 2.1.3 BACTERIAL SHAPES
notes:
✓ Bacteria are commonly classified by shape:

◆ Coccus → spherical.
◆ Bacillus → rod-shaped.
◆ Spirochaete → spiral/corkscrew-shaped.

✓ Bacterial cells may also occur singly or in characteristic arrangements such as pairs, chains or packets.

title: 2.1.4 GRAM-POSITIVE & GRAM-NEGATIVE BACTERIA
notes:
✓ Gram staining → method used to distinguish bacteria according to cell-wall properties.

✓ Gram-positive:
◆ Thick peptidoglycan layer.
◆ Retains crystal-violet stain.
◆ Appears purple.

✓ Gram-negative:
◆ Thin peptidoglycan layer.
◆ Has an outer membrane.
◆ Does not retain crystal violet and takes the counterstain.

✓ Peptidoglycan → rigid structural material of the bacterial cell wall.

title: 2.1.5 NUTRITIONAL TYPES OF BACTERIA
notes:
✓ Bacteria obtain energy and carbon in different ways.

◆ Phototrophs → obtain energy from light.
◆ Chemotrophs → obtain energy from chemical reactions.
◆ Autotrophs → obtain carbon mainly from inorganic carbon such as CO₂.
◆ Heterotrophs → obtain carbon from organic compounds.

✓ Major combinations include:
◆ Photolithoautotrophs.
◆ Photoorganoheterotrophs.
◆ Chemolithoautotrophs.
◆ Chemolithoheterotrophs.
◆ Chemoorganoheterotrophs.

title: 2.1.6 REPRODUCTION IN BACTERIA
notes:
✓ Most bacteria reproduce asexually by binary fission.

✓ Binary fission:
1 DNA replicates.
2 Chromosomes separate.
3 Cell grows and forms a cross-wall.
4 One cell divides into two genetically similar cells.

✓ Genetic exchange can also occur through processes such as conjugation.

✓ Conjugation → transfer of DNA between bacterial cells through direct contact.

title: 2.1.7 BACTERIAL DISEASES
notes:
✓ Some bacteria are pathogenic and cause diseases in humans.

✓ Examples include:
◆ Tuberculosis.
◆ Pertussis (whooping cough).
◆ Meningitis.
◆ Cholera.
◆ Typhoid fever.
◆ Syphilis.

✓ Disease transmission and prevention depend on the specific pathogen and route of transmission.

title: 2.2 ARCHAEA
notes:
✓ Archaea → unicellular prokaryotes belonging to a domain distinct from Bacteria.

◆ Lack a true nucleus.
◆ Cell walls do not contain typical bacterial peptidoglycan.
◆ Membrane structure differs from bacteria.
◆ Many live in extreme environments.
◆ Archaea have not been identified as human pathogens in the textbook.

title: 2.2.1 MAJOR GROUPS OF ARCHAEA
notes:
✓ Important ecological groups include:

◆ Extreme halophiles → live in highly saline environments.

◆ Hyperthermophiles → grow at very high temperatures, often near volcanic environments.

◆ Anaerobic archaea → live where oxygen is absent.

✓ Their unusual environments make archaea important sources of specialized enzymes.

title: 2.2.2 BENEFICIAL ASPECTS OF ARCHAEA
notes:
✓ Archaea are useful in:

◆ Production of enzymes that function under extreme conditions.
◆ Industrial processes such as high-temperature applications.
◆ Environmental biotechnology and bioremediation.
◆ Methane production in anaerobic environments.

✓ Their enzymes can be valuable because they remain functional under conditions that inhibit many other organisms.

title: 2.2.3 FACTORS AFFECTING MICROBIAL GROWTH
notes:
✓ Microbial growth is influenced by environmental conditions such as:

◆ Temperature.
◆ Moisture.
◆ Oxygen concentration.
◆ Nutrient availability.
◆ Chemical composition of the environment.
◆ pH and other physical conditions.

✓ Different microorganisms have different optimum growth conditions.

title: 2.3 FUNGI
notes:
✓ Fungi → eukaryotic organisms that include yeasts, molds and mushrooms.

◆ Have membrane-bound organelles and a nucleus.
◆ Usually obtain nutrients by absorption.
◆ Many are decomposers or parasites.
◆ Most fungi have hyphae forming a mycelium.
◆ Can reproduce sexually and asexually.

✓ Mycology → scientific study of fungi.

title: 2.3.1 FUNGAL STRUCTURE
notes:
✓ Hypha → thread-like fungal structure.

✓ Mycelium → network of hyphae.

✓ Septate hyphae → divided by cross-walls.

✓ Nonseptate/coenocytic hyphae → lack cross-walls between many nuclei.

✓ Yeasts → unicellular fungi.

✓ Hyphae provide a large surface area for absorption of nutrients.

title: 2.3.2 ECOLOGY & CLASSIFICATION OF FUNGI
notes:
✓ Fungi occur in many environments and interact with other organisms.

◆ Saprophytic fungi → obtain nutrients from dead organic matter.
◆ Parasitic fungi → obtain nutrients from living hosts.
◆ Mutualistic fungi → form beneficial relationships with other organisms.

✓ Mycorrhiza → association between fungi and plant roots.

✓ Lichen → symbiotic association involving a fungus and a photosynthetic organism.

✓ Major fungal groups presented include:
◆ Chytridiomycota.
◆ Zygomycota.
◆ Ascomycota.
◆ Basidiomycota.

title: 2.3.3 REPRODUCTION IN FUNGI
notes:
✓ Fungi reproduce both asexually and sexually.

✓ Asexual reproduction:
◆ Spore formation.
◆ Budding in yeasts.
◆ Fragmentation of hyphae.

✓ Sexual reproduction:
◆ Involves fusion of compatible fungal cells/nuclei.
◆ Often produces specialized sexual spores.
◆ Fruiting bodies may develop and produce spores.

✓ Sporulation → process of producing spores.

title: 2.3.4 ECONOMIC IMPORTANCE OF FUNGI
notes:
✓ Useful:
◆ Decompose organic matter and recycle nutrients.
◆ Used in food and beverage fermentation.
◆ Produce antibiotics and other medicines.
◆ Used to produce enzymes and organic compounds.
◆ Important in traditional fermented foods.

✓ Harmful:
◆ Cause plant diseases.
◆ Spoil agricultural products and materials.
◆ Produce mycotoxins.
◆ Cause fungal diseases in humans and animals.

title: 2.3.5 FUNGAL DISEASES
notes:
✓ Fungal disease → illness caused by pathogenic fungi.

✓ Examples:
◆ Athlete's foot.
◆ Candidiasis.
◆ Aspergillosis.
◆ Dermatophytosis.
◆ Onychomycosis → fungal infection of nails.

✓ Transmission may occur through infected people/animals, contaminated objects or airborne spores.
✓ Prevention → hygiene, keeping skin dry and avoiding contaminated personal items.

title: 2.4 PROTOZOA
notes:
✓ Protozoa → mostly unicellular eukaryotic organisms traditionally grouped among protists.

◆ Usually microscopic.
◆ Have a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.
◆ Most are heterotrophic.
◆ Some are free-living, while others are parasitic or symbiotic.
◆ Many are motile.
◆ Most reproduce asexually, but sexual processes also occur.

title: 2.4.1 NUTRITION & REPRODUCTION OF PROTOZOA
notes:
✓ Protozoa obtain food mainly by:

◆ Ingestion → taking food particles into the cell.

◆ Absorption → absorbing dissolved nutrients.

✓ Some protists obtain energy through photosynthesis.

✓ Asexual reproduction:
◆ Binary fission.
◆ Multiple fission.

✓ Sexual processes may also occur, such as conjugation in Paramecium.

title: 2.4.2 COMMON PROTOZOAL DISEASES
notes:
✓ Important protozoal diseases include:

◆ Malaria.
◆ African trypanosomiasis (sleeping sickness).
◆ Amoebiasis.
◆ Giardiasis.
◆ Chagas disease.
◆ Leishmaniasis.
◆ Toxoplasmosis.
◆ Cryptosporidiosis.

✓ Transmission may occur through contaminated food/water or vectors such as mosquitoes and tsetse flies, depending on the disease.

title: 2.5 VIRUSES
notes:
✓ Virus → extremely small, acellular infectious particle that requires a suitable host cell for replication.

◆ Not composed of a typical cellular structure.
◆ Cannot reproduce independently outside a host cell.
◆ Contain either DNA or RNA as genetic material.
◆ Surrounded by a protein coat called a capsid.
◆ Some viruses have an additional lipid envelope.

✓ Viruses are active inside host cells but may be inert outside them.

title: 2.5.1 STRUCTURE OF VIRUSES
notes:
✓ Basic viral structures:

◆ Genome → viral DNA or RNA.

◆ Capsid → protein coat surrounding the genome.

◆ Capsomeres → repeating protein units forming the capsid.

◆ Envelope → lipid-containing outer layer present in some viruses.

◆ Surface proteins → help viruses attach to specific host cells.

◆ Virion → complete virus particle outside its host cell.

title: 2.5.2 VIRAL SYMMETRY & SHAPES
notes:
✓ Major viral forms include:

◆ Helical → capsid proteins arranged in a spiral.

◆ Icosahedral/polyhedral → capsid has a geometric structure.

◆ Complex → structure does not fit simply into helical or polyhedral forms.

✓ Examples mentioned include Tobacco mosaic virus as a helical virus and pox viruses as complex viruses.

title: 2.5.3 DNA & RNA VIRUSES
notes:
✓ DNA viruses → contain DNA as genetic material.

✓ RNA viruses → contain RNA as genetic material.

✓ Viral replication depends on the type of virus and host cell.
◆ Some RNA viruses replicate in the cytoplasm.
◆ Some DNA viruses replicate in the nucleus.
◆ Retroviruses use reverse transcriptase to make DNA from an RNA template.

title: 2.5.4 VIRAL REPLICATION
notes:
✓ Major stages of viral replication:

1 Adsorption → virus attaches to the host cell.
2 Penetration → viral genetic material enters the host cell.
3 Replication/Synthesis → viral nucleic acid and proteins are produced.
4 Assembly → new virus particles are assembled.
5 Release → new virions leave the host cell.

✓ Viruses use host-cell machinery to produce new viral components.

title: 2.5.5 BACTERIOPHAGES
notes:
✓ Bacteriophage → virus that infects bacteria.

✓ Two important replication cycles:

◆ Lytic cycle → virus replicates rapidly and eventually lyses the bacterial cell.

◆ Lysogenic cycle → viral DNA becomes associated with/integrated into host DNA and replicates with the host cell before entering a productive cycle.

title: 2.5.6 VIRAL DISEASES
notes:
✓ Viral disease → disease caused by a virus.

◆ Viruses infect humans, animals and plants.
◆ Transmission varies according to the virus.
◆ Prevention may involve hygiene, vaccination, vector control, safe food/water practices and avoiding exposure to infected materials.

✓ HIV is a virus that attacks the body's immune system.

title: 2.6 NORMAL MICROBIOTA
notes:
✓ Normal microbiota → population of microorganisms normally found growing on or in healthy individuals.

✓ Resident microbiota → normally present for long periods.

✓ Transient microbiota → present temporarily.

✓ Benefits:
◆ Help prevent colonization by pathogens.
◆ Contribute to nutrient metabolism.
◆ Can stimulate the immune system.
◆ Some produce useful substances such as vitamins.

title: 2.6.1 KOCH'S POSTULATES
notes:
✓ Koch's postulates → criteria developed to establish a relationship between a microorganism and a specific disease.

✓ Core idea:
1 Microorganism is associated with diseased organisms.
2 It is isolated and studied separately.
3 The isolated organism causes the disease in a suitable healthy host.
4 The same organism is recovered again from the newly diseased host.

✓ Koch's work greatly advanced the study of infectious diseases.

title: 2.7 MODES OF DISEASE TRANSMISSION
notes:
✓ Major transmission routes include:

◆ Water/food-borne → contaminated food or water.
◆ Airborne/droplet → respiratory droplets or airborne particles.
◆ Direct contact → person-to-person contact.
◆ Indirect contact → contaminated objects/materials.
◆ Blood-borne → infected blood or contaminated needles.
◆ Sexual transmission → infected semen or vaginal secretions.
◆ Vector-borne → transmission through organisms such as mosquitoes or tsetse flies.

✓ Understanding transmission helps determine prevention methods.

title: 2.7.1 PREVENTION OF MICROBIAL DISEASES
notes:
✓ Important preventive measures:

◆ Personal and environmental hygiene.
◆ Safe food and drinking water.
◆ Proper sanitation and waste disposal.
◆ Disinfection and sterilization where appropriate.
◆ Vaccination.
◆ Vector control.
◆ Safe handling of blood and medical equipment.
◆ Avoiding contact with infectious materials.

title: 2.8 USES OF MICROORGANISMS IN AGRICULTURE
notes:
✓ Microorganisms contribute to agriculture through:

◆ Organic-matter decomposition.
◆ Nitrogen fixation.
◆ Phosphate solubilization.
◆ Potassium mobilization.
◆ Suppression of soil-borne pathogens.
◆ Degradation of toxic substances and pesticides.
◆ Production of antibiotics and other bioactive compounds.
◆ Improvement of soil structure and nutrient availability.

✓ Microorganisms are essential for maintaining soil fertility and nutrient cycling.

title: 2.8.1 MICROORGANISMS & BIOREMEDIATION
notes:
✓ Bioremediation → use of microorganisms, plants or their products to degrade, transform or remove environmental contaminants.

◆ Microbes metabolize pollutants through natural biochemical pathways.
◆ Pollutants may be transformed into less harmful substances.
◆ Microorganisms can act on hydrocarbons, pesticides, metals and other contaminants.

✓ Bioremediation → biological processes used to clean contaminated environments.

title: 2.8.2 MICROORGANISMS IN FOOD PRODUCTION
notes:
✓ Microorganisms are important in fermentation and food processing.

◆ Lactic acid bacteria → yogurt, pickles, cheeses and some fermented foods.

◆ Yeasts → bread, beer and other fermented products.

✓ Microorganisms contribute to taste, texture, preservation and aroma.

✓ Fermentation converts food substrates into useful products through microbial metabolism.

title: 2.8.3 MICROORGANISMS IN MEDICINE & BIOTECHNOLOGY
notes:
✓ Microorganisms are used to produce:

◆ Human insulin.
◆ Growth hormones.
◆ Antibiotics.
◆ Other medicines and biological products.
◆ Useful enzymes and biotechnology products.

✓ Recombinant DNA technology allows microorganisms to produce valuable human proteins.

title: 2.8.4 MICROORGANISMS & BIOGEOCHEMICAL CYCLES
notes:
✓ Microorganisms are essential in recycling elements.

◆ Carbon cycle → decomposition and carbon transformations.

◆ Nitrogen cycle → nitrogen fixation and other microbial transformations.

◆ Sulfur cycle → microbial conversion of sulfur compounds.

◆ Phosphorus cycle → decomposition and mineralization of organic phosphorus.

✓ Microorganisms convert elements into forms that can be used by other organisms.

title: 2.8.5 ANAEROBIC MICROORGANISMS & WASTEWATER
notes:
✓ Anaerobic microorganisms can be used in wastewater treatment.

◆ Help reduce sludge volume.
◆ Produce methane during anaerobic digestion.
◆ Methane can be used as an alternative energy source.
◆ Anaerobic processes can also contribute to phosphorus removal.

✓ Wastewater treatment can therefore provide both environmental and energy benefits.

title: 2.9 CONTROL OF MICROORGANISMS
notes:
✓ Sterilization → complete removal/destruction of all living microorganisms, including spores.

✓ Disinfection → destruction/removal of pathogenic microorganisms, mainly on non-living surfaces.

✓ Antisepsis → use of antimicrobial chemicals on living tissues to destroy or inhibit pathogens.

✓ Germicide/microbicide → chemical agent that kills microorganisms.

✓ Sterilization ≠ disinfection ≠ antisepsis.

title: 2.9.1 HEAT & MICROBIAL CONTROL
notes:
✓ Heat is a simple and effective method of controlling microorganisms.

✓ Pasteurization → heat treatment of liquid foods to reduce harmful microorganisms.

✓ Examples given in the textbook:

◆ Low-temperature pasteurization → 61.5°C for 30 min or 71°C for 15 sec.

◆ High-temperature pasteurization → about 80–85°C for a short period.

◆ Uperization → about 150°C for a very short period under pressure.

✓ Boiling does not necessarily achieve sterilization because some bacterial spores may survive.

title: 2.9.2 DRY & MOIST HEAT STERILIZATION
notes:
✓ Dry heat:

◆ Flaming → sterilizes small metal instruments by direct flame.

◆ Incineration → destroys infectious materials by burning.

◆ Hot-air oven → approximately 160–180°C for about 2 hours and 30 minutes.

✓ Moist heat:
◆ Autoclave → uses saturated pressurized steam.
◆ Example condition → about 120°C for 15 minutes under pressure.

✓ Moist heat is highly effective because steam transfers heat efficiently.

title: 2.9.3 TYNDALLIZATION
notes:
✓ Tyndallization → intermittent sterilization used for some heat-sensitive materials.

◆ Material is exposed to free-flowing steam at about 100°C for 20 minutes.
◆ Treatment is repeated on three consecutive days.
◆ Used when materials cannot withstand higher autoclave temperatures.

✓ The repeated heating allows resistant forms to germinate and then be destroyed during later treatments.

notes:

✓ Protozoa → mostly unicellular eukaryotic protists.

✓ Virus → acellular infectious particle requiring a host cell for replication.

✓ Gram-positive → thick peptidoglycan; purple after Gram staining.

✓ Gram-negative → thin peptidoglycan + outer membrane.

✓ Binary fission → common bacterial asexual reproduction.

✓ Hypha → thread-like fungal structure.

✓ Mycelium → network of fungal hyphae.

✓ Bacteriophage → virus that infects bacteria.

✓ Lytic cycle → viral replication ending in host-cell lysis.

✓ Lysogenic cycle → viral genetic material persists with host DNA.

✓ Normal microbiota → microorganisms normally associated with healthy individuals.

✓ Koch's postulates → criteria linking a microorganism to a disease.

✓ Sterilization → destroys/removes all microorganisms including spores.

✓ Disinfection → removes/destroys pathogens on non-living surfaces.

✓ Antisepsis → antimicrobial treatment of living tissue.

✓ Bioremediation → biological treatment of environmental pollutants.
